title: Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States
articleTitle: An In-Depth Analysis of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States: A Paradigm Shift in Research and Development Tax Credit Substantiation and Corporate Compliance
court: United States Court of Federal Claims
subject: Qualified Research Expenses
summary: Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States is a federal R&D tax credit dispute over a $1.3 million IRC Section 41 refund claim for 2018. Its key takeaway for U.S. taxpayers: retrospective SME interviews and percentage estimates, unsupported by contemporaneous time records or invoices, expose claims to full disallowance; the South Carolina suit moved to Tax Court.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Context and the Taxpayer's Refund Claim

The federal tax dispute in Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States represents a watershed confrontation between traditional accounting firm study practices and heightened Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and Department of Justice (DOJ) evidentiary enforcement under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The plaintiff, Kyocera AVX Components Corporation (formerly known as AVX Corporation), is a major multinational manufacturer of advanced passive electronic components, interconnect devices, and sensors headquartered in Fountain Inn, South Carolina, operating as a consolidated United States subsidiary of the Japanese electronics conglomerate Kyocera Corporation. Given the capital-intensive and technologically demanding nature of advanced electronic component manufacturing, Kyocera AVX routinely engaged in product development, materials science engineering, and complex manufacturing process refinement across its domestic facilities.

For its fiscal tax year ending March 31, 2018 (the 2018 tax year), Kyocera AVX timely filed (on extension, in January 2019) its original federal corporate income tax return (Form 1120), reporting a total federal income tax liability of $101,087,342. On that original return, the corporation claimed a baseline federal research and development (R&D) tax credit under IRC § 41 of $398,985. Subsequent to the original filing, on August 19, 2019 (more than sixteen months after the close of the tax year at issue), Kyocera AVX retained PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), a Big Four accounting firm, to conduct a comprehensive, multi-year look-back R&D tax credit study covering the 2017 through 2020 tax years. Relying on the findings of the retrospective PwC study, Kyocera AVX filed, in July 2021, an amended federal income tax return for the 2018 tax year claiming a revised total Section 41 research credit of approximately $1.7 million ($1,709,147), which generated an incremental research credit refund claim of $1,310,162 (frequently cited in litigation filings as approximately $1.3 million), based on claimed qualified research expenses of $23,186,512 in employee wages, $1,460,503 in supplies, and $320,031 in contract research. When more than six months elapsed from the filing date of the administrative refund claim without a formal determination by the IRS, Kyocera AVX exercised its statutory right under IRC §§ 6532(a)(1) and 7422(a) to initiate a civil tax refund lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina on July 28, 2022, docketed as Case No. 6:22-cv-02440-TMC before Chief Judge Timothy M. Cain.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

The substantive legal battle in Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States is governed by the interlocking provisions of IRC §§ 41, 174, 6001, and 7422, alongside the corresponding Treasury Regulations. Under IRC § 41(a), a taxpayer is entitled to a credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over the base amount, or 14 percent of QREs exceeding 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years under the Alternative Simplified Credit of IRC § 41(c)(4). Total QREs under IRC § 41(b) consist of in-house research expenses (wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and amounts paid for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)) and 65 percent of contract research expenses paid or incurred to any person other than an employee for qualified research under § 41(b)(3).

For underlying activities to constitute "qualified research," the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving that each claimed project satisfies the conjunctive Four-Part Test codified in IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a). First, under the Section 174 Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, meaning the costs must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Second, under the Technological Information Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)), the taxpayer must intend to apply that discovered information to the development of a new or improved business component—defined under § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)), substantially all of the activities of the research must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, expressed mathematically as:

In addition to satisfying the substantive elements of IRC § 41, every taxpayer claiming a research credit is bound by the overarching substantiation mandate of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a), which require taxpayers to keep permanent books of account or records, including inventories, as are sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown by such person in any return of such tax. More specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) mandates that a taxpayer claiming a credit under Section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit.

In the District of South Carolina litigation, the United States mounted a two-stage offensive against Kyocera AVX's refund suit. Initially, on December 6, 2022, the DOJ filed a Motion to Dismiss pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1), arguing that the District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the full-payment rule established by the U.S. Supreme Court in Flora v. United States, 362 U.S. 145 (1960). Because Kyocera AVX had elected under IRC § 965(h) to pay its Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) transition tax liability in eight annual installments, it had remitted only $64,857,236 toward the $101,087,342 total tax liability reported on its original FY 2018 return as of July 2020. The government contended that because the § 965 transition tax is not a divisible tax and Congress enacted no statutory exception to Flora for § 965(h) installment elections, the taxpayer had not fully paid its assessed 2018 income tax liability prior to filing suit.

Subsequently, following extensive discovery regarding the merits of the R&D tax credit claim, the United States filed a Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on July 19, 2024 (ECF No. 77), seeking summary judgment on Count I of the amended complaint and disallowance of Kyocera AVX's Section 41 credit claim in its entirety; although the refund sought was only the $1,310,162 increment, the government argued that Kyocera AVX bore the burden of establishing eligibility for the entire $1,709,147 credit. The government asserted that no genuine dispute of material fact existed because Kyocera AVX failed to satisfy its burden of proof under IRC § 41 and the recordkeeping requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d). Specifically, the DOJ argued that the PwC study relied exclusively on retrospective interviews and uncorroborated percentage estimates from just 36 Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) to quantify the activities of roughly 1,200 employees, was not supported by contemporaneous time tracking (Kyocera AVX had no centralized time-tracking system and generally did not track employee time on projects) or other retained records, failed to validate supply and contract research expenses with underlying invoices, and could not be tested because Kyocera AVX produced no documents beyond the PwC study in response to the government's requests for production, while PwC, in response to the government's subpoena, produced only workpaper spreadsheets and had retained neither the survey responses nor the questions asked during its SME interviews.
Procedural Trajectory and Judicial Holdings

Analyzing the judicial disposition of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States requires distinguishing between several separate federal proceedings involving the taxpayer and tracing the jurisdictional migration of the Section 41 dispute from the U.S. District Court to the U.S. Tax Court. First, in an earlier, distinct action before the United States Court of Federal Claims—Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States, No. 1:21-cv-02146, 165 Fed. Cl. 110 (decided March 28, 2023)—Chief Judge Elaine D. Kaplan granted Kyocera AVX's Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings (granting the government's cross-motion only as to deficiency-interest offsets), holding under Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. United States, 417 F.3d 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2005), that the two-year limitations period of 26 U.S.C. §§ 6532(b) and 7405 barred the IRS from offsetting approximately $1.34 million of excess overpayment interest paid in 2017 against refunds for the tax years ending March 31, 2007 and 2008, and rejecting the government's equitable recoupment argument; the government's subsequent appeal was dismissed by agreement of the parties under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit on October 2, 2023.

Second, in the primary R&D tax credit refund litigation before the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina (Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States, No. 6:22-cv-02440-TMC), the procedural trajectory took a decisive turn following the briefing on the government's July 19, 2024 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment. Before the District Court issued a substantive ruling on the summary judgment motion, the IRS issued a statutory Notice of Deficiency asserting an additional $2.3 million income tax deficiency against Kyocera AVX for the 2018 tax year. Furthermore, on March 12, 2025, the United States filed a separate new lawsuit against Kyocera AVX in the District of South Carolina, alleging that the corporation had received a $13.36 million tax refund for the 2018 tax year in error and owed the government $13.36 million plus statutory interest. In response to the deficiency determination, Kyocera AVX filed a petition in the United States Tax Court in March 2025 to contest the deficiency assessment, thereby incorporating its Section 41 research credit refund claim into the Tax Court proceeding.

Consequently, on April 1, 2025, Chief Judge Timothy M. Cain, following the parties' joint status report (ECF No. 110), entered judgment (ECF No. 112) dismissing the South Carolina District Court action (No. 6:22-cv-02440-TMC), agreeing with both parties that the court lacked jurisdiction once Kyocera AVX had petitioned the U.S. Tax Court regarding its 2018 tax liability (consistent with the concurrent-litigation rule of IRC § 7422(e)), so that the disputed issues would proceed in the Tax Court. While rigorous legal analysis requires noting that a litigant's summary judgment motion is not itself a merits holding and Chief Judge Cain's April 1, 2025 order disposed of the District Court suit on jurisdictional grounds rather than establishing a new judicial ban on retrospective evidence, the evidentiary record exposed in Kyocera AVX—and the controlling appellate and Tax Court precedents invoked by the government, notably Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) and Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), and Moore v. Commissioner, 101 F.4th 509 (7th Cir. 2024)—articulates the uncompromising standard of proof that governs large-enterprise Section 41 claims across all federal tax tribunals.

body.text: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Disproportionate SME Extrapolation and Federal Rule of Evidence 802 Hearsay Vulnerabilities

The foundational defect that triggered the government's summary judgment offensive in Kyocera AVX was the extreme statistical and evidentiary disconnect between the breadth of the employee population claimed and the narrow pool of witnesses interviewed to substantiate those claims. In constructing the multi-year look-back study for tax years 2017 through 2020, PwC relied almost exclusively on retrospective interviews and survey responses gathered from just 36 Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) to evaluate, reconstruct, and quantify the daily activities of approximately 1,200 employees across Kyocera AVX's operations. The government argued that, at this roughly 1-to-33 ratio between SMEs and claimed personnel, the interviewees were estimating the time of too large a group to possess sufficient knowledge, diminishing the reliability of the study under both substantive federal tax law and the Federal Rules of Evidence.

In federal refund litigation, the taxpayer must present admissible evidence sufficient to survive summary judgment under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56. Under Federal Rule of Evidence (FRE) 602, a lay witness may testify to a matter only if evidence is introduced sufficient to support a finding that the witness has personal knowledge of the matter. In Kyocera AVX, the 36 SMEs were asked not merely to describe their own work, but to estimate the time spent by other employees in their departments, over 1,200 employees in total, including employees up and down the organizational hierarchy; for example, frontline managers provided estimates of time spent not only by their direct reports but also by senior executives such as the Chief Operating Officer. Furthermore, the DOJ argued that the PwC study rests on multiple layers of hearsay (the study itself, the SMEs' survey statements, and the SMEs' likely second-hand knowledge of other employees' time), so that under FRE 805 each layer must satisfy a hearsay exception. Because the accounting firm's study consisted of out-of-court assertions compiled after the tax years had closed by third-party consultants summarizing unverified oral statements of employees for the truth of the matter asserted—and neither existed as a record of a regularly conducted activity made at or near the time of the engineering events under the business records exception of FRE 803(6) nor was supported by underlying primary documentation—the government contended that, even if the 36 SMEs had personal knowledge of their own time, they lacked a non-hearsay foundation for how the remaining 1,167 employees named in the study spent their time, so the study could not be put in admissible form for trial or serve as a basis for a Cohan estimate.

Compounding this hearsay and personal-knowledge failure was the improper treatment of employee job titles and organizational hierarchies. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), "qualified services" are strictly limited to engaging in qualified research (direct performance), engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research, or engaging in the direct support of research activities. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) specifies that "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, such as a laboratory scientist who directly supervises a research group, and explicitly excludes higher-level managers to whom first-line managers report, even if those executives are qualified scientists or engineers. In Kyocera AVX, the retrospective SME allocations swept in upper-level management and support personnel without granular, activity-level evidence proving that those individuals performed hands-on experimentation or immediate first-line technical supervision rather than general administrative oversight or commercial production support.
Absence of Contemporaneous Time Tracking and Failure to Prove the 80 Percent Process of Experimentation Threshold

Closely intertwined with the flawed SME survey architecture was Kyocera AVX's lack of contemporaneous time tracking for the claimed research projects: it had no centralized system for tracking employee time and generally did not track employee time on projects, although it did track time for certain military and government contracts that were not part of the claim. Instead of presenting system-generated timesheets, project-level labor logs, or real-time engineering ticket data linking specific employee hours to discrete research projects, the taxpayer relied on retrospective percentage estimates solicited during the post-period PwC interviews—for example, the study concluded that a Technical Marketing Manager spent 80 percent of his time on qualified research for the Ceramic Components business component and, because PwC applied the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold per employee rather than per business component, claimed 100 percent of his wages, while comparable after-the-fact estimates were assigned to an Administrative Assistant (80 percent), a Quality Manager (70 percent), a President (50 percent), and a Planner (50 percent).

Both the IRS and federal courts have systematically dismantled claims resting on uncorroborated percentage reconstructions because such estimates cannot satisfy the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). As crystallized by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and reinforced by the government's reliance on Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014) (holding employee testimony insufficient to substantiate time spent on qualified services), a taxpayer must provide a principled, verifiable method to establish that at least 80 percent of all research activities applied to a specific business component constituted elements of a process of experimentation. When an SME offers an arbitrary, macro-level percentage estimate of an employee's annual time without tying those hours to specific business components and separating true experimental iterations from routine engineering, commercial adaptation, debugging, or post-production quality control, the court has no factual denominator or numerator with which to verify the 80 percent threshold.

Crucially, the litigation record in Kyocera AVX underscores why taxpayers cannot rely on the judicial estimation doctrine of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to salvage undocumented percentage allocations. As Little Sandy Coal explicitly held, a court or the IRS may estimate the amount of qualified research expenses only after the taxpayer has first proven through reliable records that qualified research actually occurred under the Section 41(d) Four-Part Test, including proof that the 80 percent process of experimentation threshold was met for the specific business component. Using arbitrary time estimates to prove the threshold element of qualification itself—namely, whether 80 percent of the research activities were experimental—is legally impermissible. Without real-time or project-contemporaneous records demonstrating which specific projects, which specific activities, and which specific hours met the Section 41 criteria, retrospective approximations fail as a matter of law.
Overbroad Business Component Definitions and Failure to Isolate Technological Uncertainty

A third critical technical deficiency in Kyocera AVX stemmed from the failure to define business components at an appropriate level of granularity and to link those components to documented technological uncertainty and structured experimentation. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), the Four-Part Test must be applied separately to each business component of the taxpayer. When a taxpayer defines its business components overly broadly—such as grouping entire commercial product families, facility-wide manufacturing lines, or standard customer part modifications into a single monolithic component—it invites catastrophic disqualification under the "all-or-nothing" mechanics of the 80 percent rule. If more than 20 percent of the activities associated with that broadly defined component involve routine pre-production planning, commercial tooling setup, vendor qualification, or validation testing against customer specifications, the entire business component fails the process of experimentation test.

To mitigate this risk, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) provides the "shrinking-back rule," which dictates that if a broad product or process fails the Four-Part Test at the macro level, the requirements are then applied at the most significant subset of elements of the product or process (the subcomponent level), continuing down to the discrete element where the uncertainty and experimentation actually occurred. However, a taxpayer can invoke the shrinking-back rule only if its documentation segregates both the technical experimentation and the associated employee wages and supply costs at the subcomponent level. Because Kyocera AVX relied on high-level SME interviews that allocated employee time to five broadly drawn business components (Tantalum Components, Ceramic Components, Advanced Specialty, Antenna, and Interconnect) without retaining contemporaneous project artifacts—such as engineering design documents, CAD iterations, laboratory test protocols, failure mode analyses, and hypothesis-driven test results—the government argued that it could neither substantiate that its macro-level components met the Four-Part Test nor shrink back its claim to discrete, qualifying subcomponents. Furthermore, in the absence of technical documentation proving that the capability, method, or appropriate design of the component was uncertain at the outset of the work under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), the government argued that the study included wages of employees in technical sales, manufacturing, and quality control without substantiating their research activities, noting that Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5) excludes quality control work from qualified research and that the study offered no description of the tasks employees performed or of how qualifying experimentation was distinguished from non-qualified activities.
Unsubstantiated Supply Expenses, Pilot Models, and Contract Research Exclusions

The evidentiary breakdown in Kyocera AVX extended beyond employee wages to infect the taxpayer's claimed supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and contract research QREs under IRC § 41(b)(3). In its summary judgment motion, the DOJ showed from the discovery record that PwC applied the same post-period interview and estimation framework, starting from Kyocera AVX's general ledger account balances, to allocate supply expenses ($1,460,503 claimed) and contract research expenses ($320,031 claimed) to particular projects years after the expenses were incurred, that the study did not identify supply expenses on a per-invoice or per-order level and PwC never requested that documentation, and that Kyocera AVX produced no supply invoices or contract invoices.

In the context of complex industrial manufacturing, claiming supply QREs requires navigating the strict boundary between experimental pilot models and routine commercial production expenses. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b), "supplies" mean any tangible property other than land or improvements to land and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), the costs of producing a "pilot model"—defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product, including a fully-functional representation produced at a single or multiple copy scale—can qualify as research expenditures. However, once uncertainty regarding the capability, method, or design is resolved, or when materials are consumed in routine manufacturing, commercial production runs, or quality control testing to verify that units meet established customer specifications (as highlighted in Little Sandy Coal and Betz v. Commissioner), those expenditures are statutorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) (research after commercial production) and § 41(d)(4)(D) (efficiency surveys and routine quality control). Because Kyocera AVX produced no supply invoices and the PwC study did not identify supply expenses on a per-invoice or per-order level (pilot-model and bill-of-materials issues were not addressed in the government's motion), the government argued that Kyocera AVX could not demonstrate that its claimed supply expenses were consumed directly in qualified research rather than routine manufacturing.

Similarly, the government emphasized that Kyocera AVX produced no invoices supporting its contract research expenses, which the SMEs had allocated to projects by post-hoc estimate (the government's motion did not separately raise the vendor-agreement requirements or the funded research exclusion discussed below). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research by a third party only to the extent that it is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, provides that research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. Conversely, when a manufacturer develops custom components for original equipment manufacturer (OEM) customers, the taxpayer must prove that its own engineering activities are not excluded as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). As established in federal decisions such as Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, and Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, a taxpayer's customer-commissioned research is disqualified as funded unless the governing contracts explicitly place financial risk on the taxpayer (making payment contingent on technical research success and subject to rejection or uncompensated rework) and leave the taxpayer with "substantial rights" in the resulting technology. Without producing contractor invoices, statements of work, or customer contracts during discovery, a taxpayer cannot satisfy either the affirmative criteria of § 41(b)(3) or negate the funded research exclusion of § 41(d)(4)(H).
Violation of IRC Section 6001 Recordkeeping Mandates and Discovery Spoliation Risks

Perhaps the most damaging revelation in the Kyocera AVX litigation occurred during formal discovery, when the DOJ served requests for production on Kyocera AVX and a subpoena on PwC for the foundational records underlying the $1,310,162 refund claim. In response, Kyocera AVX produced no time-tracking documents, supply invoices, or contract invoices, and PwC produced only internal workpaper spreadsheets that aggregated and summarized survey data; PwC had retained neither the survey responses nor even the questions asked during its SME interviews, and never provided the completed surveys to Kyocera AVX. Kyocera AVX produced no documents beyond the PwC study itself to substantiate its $1.7 million total credit claim; notably, PwC's engagement letter stated that PwC and Kyocera AVX would discuss the retention and storage of contemporaneous documentation, but that discussion never took place.

In its summary judgment briefing, the United States argued that Kyocera AVX's failure to create or retain contemporaneous documentation, project time-tracking data, and the underlying survey responses left it unable to meet the requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) that a taxpayer claiming a Section 41 credit retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate eligibility (the government did not allege affirmative destruction of records). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(e), required books and records must be retained so long as the contents thereof may become material in the administration of any internal revenue law. When a taxpayer files an amended return claiming millions of dollars in look-back tax credits and subsequently initiates federal refund litigation, the materiality of the underlying technical artifacts, financial invoices, and survey source data is absolute. Destroying or failing to preserve those primary records deprives the government of the ability to audit or cross-examine the factual basis of the consultant's summary report, which, the government argued, required the Court to disallow the credit in its entirety and to decline any Cohan estimate.
Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements, Taxpayer Deficiencies, and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory and evidentiary requirement implicated in Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States against the specific deficiencies identified in the taxpayer's study and the governing judicial standard of proof enforced by federal courts.

Requires invoice-level validation and shop-order segregation proving materials were consumed in experimental pilot models resolving design uncertainty prior to commercial production, not routine manufacturing or QA.
Contract Research QREs & Funded Research Exclusion
IRC § 41(b)(3), § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), § 1.41-4A(d); MBJ; Geosyntec; Populous Holdings
Claimed contract research expenses ($320,031) via post-hoc SME estimates without producing any contract invoices (the funded research exclusion was not raised in the government's motion).

Requires invoice-level proof and written agreements executed prior to research showing work was done on taxpayer's behalf at taxpayer's financial risk, plus contract review proving payment is contingent on technical success and taxpayer retains substantial rights.
Refund Suit Subject Matter Jurisdiction & Exclusivity
Filed District Court refund suit while paying § 965 transition tax in installments ($64.86M paid of $101.09M assessed); subsequently petitioned U.S. Tax Court after receiving $2.3M deficiency notice.

Under Flora, full payment of assessed tax is required for District Court jurisdiction; under IRC § 7422(e), petitioning the U.S. Tax Court following a deficiency notice divests the District Court of jurisdiction in favor of exclusive Tax Court jurisdiction.

body.text: As the comparative synthesis demonstrates, the evidentiary failures in Kyocera AVX were not isolated administrative oversights; rather, they formed a mutually reinforcing chain of non-compliance. When a corporate taxpayer fails to define business components at the subcomponent level and lacks contemporaneous project time tracking, it is forced to rely on retrospective SME percentage estimates. When the taxpayer attempts to minimize internal disruption by interviewing only 36 SMEs to estimate the time of over 1,200 employees and fails to archive the underlying technical artifacts, supply invoices, and survey records, the resulting study becomes vulnerable, as the government argued in this case, to exclusion as multi-level hearsay under FRE 805 and cannot demonstrate the 80 percent threshold applied in Little Sandy Coal.
Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the doctrinal lessons of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States and its governing precedents into actionable compliance architecture, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic enterprise scenarios facing the exact legal and technical pitfalls exposed in the litigation. Each case study details a step-by-step remediation blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contract structuring, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Advanced Passive Electronic Component and Multilayer Ceramic Capacitor Manufacturer
Industry Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

A domestic manufacturer of high-reliability multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) and polymer tantalum capacitors for electric vehicle (EV) power inverters employs 1,100 engineering, metallurgical, and manufacturing personnel across three U.S. fabrication plants. During the tax year, the company undertakes a major initiative ("Project Volt-Shield") to develop a next-generation high-voltage, ultra-low equivalent series resistance (ESR) ceramic capacitor capable of operating continuously at without dielectric breakdown or thermal runaway. In preparing its Section 41 R&D credit claim for $1.6 million, the company's tax department replicates the exact errors of Kyocera AVX. First, it defines the entire "Project Volt-Shield EV Capacitor Line" as a single monolithic business component. Second, lacking an engineering time-tracking system, its outside consultant interviews 30 plant managers and department directors to estimate the R&D allocation percentages for all 1,100 employees, sweeps in Plant Vice Presidents and Quality Control Inspectors at flat 35 percent allocations, and discards the raw interview notes after generating a summary PDF report. Third, the company claims $4.2 million in supply QREs by applying a 25 percent SME estimate to the entire barium titanate ceramic powder and nickel electrode paste general ledger accounts, blending experimental lab batches with full-scale commercial qualification runs without pulling a single vendor invoice.
Step 1: Project Governance and Shrinking-Back Business Component Architecture

To remediate the overbroad business component vulnerability and prevent an "all-or-nothing" disallowance under Little Sandy Coal, the tax and engineering leadership must restructure Project Volt-Shield's governance prior to or during the tax year by disaggregating the macro product line into discrete, technically autonomous subcomponents within the company's Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems. Specifically, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), Project Volt-Shield is partitioned into four distinct subcomponent project codes: Subcomponent VS-01 (Rare-Earth Doped Barium Titanate Dielectric Slurry Formulation), Subcomponent VS-02 (High-Aspect-Ratio Internal Nickel Electrode Screen-Printing Process), Subcomponent VS-03 (Reducing-Atmosphere Co-Sintering Thermal Profile), and Subcomponent VS-04 (Flexible Conductive Epoxy Termination Chemistry).

Each subcomponent is governed by a formal New Product Introduction (NPI) Stage-Gate charter that explicitly delineates when experimental R&D begins (Gate 1: Concept & Technical Uncertainty Definition) and when commercial production readiness is achieved (Gate 4: Process Validation & Commercial Release). Any activities occurring after Gate 4—such as commercial yield optimization, customer part-number adaptation, or routine statistical process control (SPC)—are automatically routed to a non-qualifying ERP cost center, ensuring that routine manufacturing never contaminates the experimental activity pool. Furthermore, the company establishes a strict SME governance rule: no SME may validate activities for more than 12 to 15 direct reports, and only first-line engineering supervisors who personally review daily laboratory results and bench tests are designated as SMEs, completely eliminating the 1-to-33 extrapolation defect and FRE 602 personal-knowledge failure of Kyocera AVX. Upper-level executives (Plant Vice Presidents and Directors who supervise first-line managers) are categorically excluded from automatic percentage allocations unless they log direct, hands-on metallurgical modeling hours in the engineering tracking system.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and IRC Section 6001 Retention Protocol

To cure the absence of contemporaneous technical records and eliminate IRC § 6001 spoliation risk, the company mandates that every subcomponent code in the PLM system maintain a structured "Section 41 Technical Dossier" populated in real time as engineering work progresses. At Gate 1 of Subcomponent VS-01, materials scientists must complete a mandatory digital field stating the exact technological uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1): for example, that existing dysprosium-doped barium titanate formulations suffer grain-boundary degradation above under a DC bias field, and that standard sintering curves cannot achieve theoretical density without inducing oxygen vacancies.

As iterative work proceeds through Gates 2 and 3, the PLM system automatically archives time-stamped design of experiments (DOE) matrices, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) micrographs of failed dielectric layers, Weibull breakdown voltage distributions, and iterative formula revisions. Crucially, the corporate tax department collaborates with Information Technology (IT) and Legal to institute an automated "Tax Credit Litigation Hold and Archival Policy". At the close of each quarter, all PLM engineering artifacts, laboratory notebooks, email threads tagged to VS-01 through VS-04, and raw SME survey exports are written to an immutable, WORM (Write Once, Read Many) cloud storage repository indexed by tax year and subcomponent ID, ensuring complete subpoena readiness under IRC § 6001 for a minimum of ten years.
Step 3: Contract Terms and Invoice-Level Supply and Pilot Model Segregation

To overcome the supply and contract research substantiation failures exposed in Kyocera AVX and Betz, the company overhauls its ERP procurement and work-order accounting workflows. Rather than estimating supply QREs via SME percentages applied to bulk raw material accounts, the ERP system is configured to require an "Experimental Pilot-Lot Work Order" (prefixed EXP-WO-) whenever materials are requisitioned from inventory or purchased externally for Subcomponents VS-01 through VS-04 prior to Gate 4 commercial release. When a ceramic engineer requisitions 50 kilograms of high-purity nanoscale powder and holmium oxide dopants to fabricate 5,000 experimental prototype capacitors for destructive high-temperature accelerated life testing (HALT), the requisition is digitally linked to the vendor's PDF commercial invoice, purchase order, receiving slip, and payment voucher.

Each EXP-WO- record explicitly documents the pilot model qualification criteria under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4): it records the hypothesis being tested by the pilot lot, confirms that the prototype units are destroyed during dielectric breakdown testing or scrapped after electrical characterization, and certifies that zero units from the lot are sold or placed into commercial finished-goods inventory. For outside metallurgical characterization and third-party synchrotron X-ray diffraction testing claimed as contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3), the Procurement and Tax departments implement a mandatory "Pre-Performance R&D Vendor Rider" attached to every purchase order. This rider explicitly stipulates prior to the commencement of work that the testing is performed on behalf of the taxpayer to resolve specified technical uncertainties of Subcomponent VS-01, vests sole ownership of all test data and intellectual property in the taxpayer, and obligates the taxpayer to pay for the laboratory services regardless of whether the experimental ceramic formulation succeeds or fails, with every vendor invoice linked directly to the subcomponent ledger.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation and Time Tracking

To replace the legally defective post-period percentage estimates and rigorously satisfy the 80 percent process of experimentation rule of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Little Sandy Coal, the company integrates a bi-weekly project time-tracking module into its engineering workflow and Jira project management environment. Engineers and technicians working on Project Volt-Shield log their hours contemporaneously against specific subcomponent codes (VS-01 through VS-04) and select from standardized activity tags mapped directly to the statutory classification under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Qualifying experimental tags include EXP-HYP (Hypothesis & DOE Formulation), EXP-MOD (Simulation & Dielectric Modeling), EXP-PRO (Pilot-Lot Fabrication & Sintering Trials), and EXP-TST (Destructive HALT & Failure Analysis), while non-experimental research or support tags include NON-LIT (Background Literature Review), NON-TOL (Commercial Tooling Calibration), and NON-QAC (Routine Customer Specification Verification).

At the end of the tax year, the tax team extracts the exact hourly ledger for each subcomponent to compute the "substantially all" ratio mathematically. For example, if Subcomponent VS-01 accumulated 8,400 hours of tagged EXP- activities out of 9,600 total research hours applied to that subcomponent ( ), the subcomponent independently satisfies the threshold under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), allowing 100 percent of the directly linked W-2 qualified wages for VS-01 to enter the QRE calculation. Conversely, if Subcomponent VS-04 (Termination Chemistry) recorded only 62 percent experimental hours due to extensive commercial vendor qualification, VS-04 is automatically excluded from the claim without jeopardizing the qualified status of VS-01, VS-02, and VS-03. Supplemental SME interviews are conducted strictly at year-end to contextualize the contemporaneous technical logs—"paving the road with documentation and filling the potholes with interviews"—with every signed SME affidavit and digital timestamp archived permanently in the audit file.
Case Study 2: Custom Aerospace and Defense Avionics Systems Integrator
Industry Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

A mid-sized aerospace and defense engineering contractor employing 450 hardware, firmware, and systems engineers designs custom radiation-hardened flight control computers and embedded fault-tolerant software for commercial satellite primes and defense OEMs. Seeking to claim $1.2 million in federal R&D tax credits across amended and current returns, the company faces severe legal exposure mirroring both Kyocera AVX and the funded-research precedents of Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (MBJ) and Geosyntec. First, the company's engineering teams operate under 18 different customer Master Services Agreements (MSAs) that blend time-and-materials (T&M), cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF), and firm-fixed-price (FFP) billing, yet the company's tax credit provider claims all 18 projects without reviewing the underlying contracts to determine whether the company bore financial risk or retained substantial rights. Second, rather than extracting real-time software and hardware engineering data from the company's Jira and GitHub repositories, the tax advisor relies on retrospective questionnaires completed by 12 Chief Engineers to estimate time across all 450 staff, assigning 50 percent R&D allocations to Systems Integration Managers, Technical Writers, and Scrum Masters based solely on job titles.
Step 1: Project Governance and Role-Based Qualification Architecture

To eliminate the job-title presumption defects and SME overreach identified in Kyocera AVX, the aerospace integrator establishes a formal "Cross-Functional R&D Tax Governance Committee" comprising the Vice President of Engineering, General Counsel, Controller, and Tax Director. The committee institutes a strict role-based qualification matrix under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) that strips away all title-based assumptions. Under this protocol, employees in non-core or ambiguous job classifications—including Program Managers, Scrum Masters, Configuration Management Specialists, Technical Writers, and Quality Assurance (QA) Engineers—are assigned a default QRE allocation of zero percent.

For any hour worked by a support or supervisory employee to be included as a qualified service under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c), the time entry must be linked to a specific experimental task ticket and corroborated by contemporaneous evidence of either "direct supervision" (first-line technical direction of an experimental test, such as a Lead Avionics Architect modifying a radiation-mitigation circuit schematic alongside a junior engineer) or "direct support" (hands-on fabrication of an experimental FPGA test fixture or execution of a thermal-vacuum chamber test script, explicitly excluding administrative scheduling, documentation formatting, or ISO/AS9100 compliance auditing). Furthermore, SME review authority is decentralized to the individual Integrated Product Team (IPT) Leads who directly supervise no more than 8 to 10 engineers on a specific hardware board or software module, ensuring that every SME possesses unimpeachable first-hand personal knowledge under FRE 602.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Automated Repository Artifact Capture

To replace retrospective narrative reconstructions with contemporaneous, system-generated proof of technological uncertainty and experimentation, the company reconfigures its existing Jira issue-tracking software and GitHub Enterprise version-control platform. Rather than treating avionics development as a single project per customer contract, each contract is decomposed into granular technical business components corresponding to discrete hardware assemblies (such as Component FC-101: Triple-Modular-Redundant SpaceVPX Processor Card) and embedded software algorithms (such as Component SW-204: Autonomous Single-Event Upset Scrubbing Kernel).

Within Jira, the engineering workflow is modified so that no "Epic" or "Story" under a research component can be opened without populating three mandatory custom metadata fields: first, a Baseline_Capability_Gap field documenting why standard off-the-shelf radiation shielding or existing error-correcting code algorithms cannot meet the required total ionizing dose threshold within a 15-watt power envelope; second, a Design_Alternatives_Matrix field listing at least two competing architectural hypotheses under evaluation; and third, an Experimental_Test_Method field linking to the hardware-in-the-loop simulation, cyclotron heavy-ion beam test plan, or Monte Carlo radiation transport model. As software and firmware engineers commit code in GitHub, commit messages automatically require the corresponding Jira ticket ID, creating an immutable, time-stamped digital audit trail linking every line of experimental code, failed compilation, timing-closure failure, and hardware bench rework directly to the underlying scientific hypothesis.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring for Financial Risk and Substantial Rights

To inoculate the claim against the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) in strict accordance with Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Geosyntec, and Populous Holdings, the General Counsel and Tax Director institute a mandatory pre-execution contract review and redrafting protocol for all customer MSAs and Statements of Work (SOWs). Initially, any SOW structured on a pure time-and-materials (T&M) or cost-plus basis where the customer reimburses engineering hours regardless of technical outcome is immediately flagged as "Funded / Disqualified" in the ERP system and excluded from the Section 41 calculation.

For custom avionics development contracts where the company seeks to preserve Section 41 eligibility, the legal team restructures the commercial agreements into Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) Technical Milestone Contracts containing four explicit legal provisions. First, regarding conditional payment contingent on technical success, progress payments and final contract consideration are legally conditioned upon the prototype hardware and software successfully passing rigorous, objective Preliminary Design Review (PDR), Critical Design Review (CDR), and Qualification Acceptance Testing (QAT) performance metrics. Second, through rejection, cure, and refund remedies, if the developed avionics component fails to meet the specified radiation-tolerance or latency parameters during QAT, the customer holds the explicit contractual right to reject the deliverable, withhold milestone payments, and demand either uncompensated engineering redesign at the contractor's sole expense or a full refund of prior milestone advances, thereby establishing genuine financial risk. Third, to preserve retained substantial rights in background and foreground intellectual property, rather than assigning exclusive ownership of all resulting designs, schematics, and algorithms to the customer without restriction, the IP clause is drafted so that the taxpayer retains ownership of (or an irrevocable, royalty-free, non-exclusive commercial license to use) all underlying architectural designs, radiation-mitigation techniques, and firmware libraries in future projects for other aerospace customers without paying royalties to the commissioning client. Fourth, under an invoice and milestone mapping protocol, every customer billing invoice and internal cost ledger is mapped to the specific contract clause demonstrating financial risk and retained rights.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Form 6765 Audit-Ready Substantiation

To synthesize the technical, contractual, and financial streams into an unimpeachable substantiation package that satisfies both judicial scrutiny and the expanded business-component reporting mandates of the revised IRS Form 6765, the company deploys an automated data-extraction pipeline linking its ERP payroll ledger, Deltek/DCAA-compliant timekeeping system, and Jira/GitHub engineering databases. Because aerospace engineers log their hours daily into a Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA)-compliant timekeeping system tied to specific work breakdown structure (WBS) codes, the company maps each qualifying WBS code directly to the corresponding Jira subcomponent (FC-101, SW-204).

Each month, an automated script reconciles the daily time-card hours against the Jira experimental ticket logs (EXP- vs. NON-EXP- activities) to verify in real time whether each subcomponent is tracking above the 80 percent process of experimentation threshold. When an IPT Lead reviews and signs off on the quarterly subcomponent technical summary, the system compiles a self-contained "Subcomponent Substantiation Binder" containing the executed FFP customer contract and IP analysis, the W-2 payroll registers and daily time-card exports for each participating engineer, the complete Jira/GitHub experimental iteration history and test logs, all vendor supply and sub-tier testing invoices with proof of payment, and the digitally signed, time-stamped SME verification. Nothing relies on retrospective memory or uncorroborated percentage estimates, completely neutralizing the substantiation vulnerabilities that the government targeted in its summary judgment motion in Kyocera AVX.

cells: Business Component Definition
Overbroad, facility-wide or macro product line groupings; vulnerable to "all-or-nothing" failure.
Disaggregated in PLM/ERP into discrete subcomponents (slurry formulation, electrode printing, sintering profile) under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
Partitioned by hardware board assembly (FC-101) and embedded software kernel (SW-204) linked to discrete WBS codes.
SME Selection & Personal Knowledge
36 SMEs estimating time for 1,200+ staff (about 1:33), including senior executives; argued to be multi-level hearsay (FRE 805).
Capped at 1:12–15 ratio; restricted strictly to first-line lab supervisors with direct daily oversight; upper executives excluded.
Decentralized to IPT Leads managing 8–10 engineers; zero-percent default for Program Managers, QA, and support roles absent direct task logs.
Time Tracking & 80% Rule Proof
No centralized time tracking on claimed projects; retrospective per-employee estimates (e.g., 80% for a Technical Marketing Manager) incapable of proving the threshold.
Bi-weekly phase-gate time logging with EXP- vs. NON- activity tags; mathematical verification of threshold per subcomponent.
Daily DCAA-compliant timecards integrated with Jira/GitHub commits; automated monthly calculation of experimental activity ratios.
Supply & Contract QRE Substantiation
Retrospective SME estimates applied to GL accounts; zero supply or contractor invoices retained; routine manufacturing mixed with R&D.
Dedicated EXP-WO- pilot-lot work orders linked to PDF vendor invoices and scrap/destruction certificates; Pre-Performance R&D Vendor Riders.
Contract-by-contract legal review; exclusion of T&M/cost-plus SOWs; FFP milestone restructuring with rejection remedies and retained IP rights.
IRC § 6001 Record Retention
Failure to create or retain contemporaneous records and raw survey responses; produced nothing beyond the consultant study.
Automated quarterly archival of PLM DOE matrices, SEM micrographs, failure logs, and raw survey data to immutable WORM cloud storage.
Real-time capture of Jira uncertainty fields, GitHub commit histories, test scripts, contracts, and signed IPT affidavits in audit-ready binders.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Federal R&D Tax Credit Practice

The litigation trajectory of Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States—stretching from the December 2022 Flora jurisdictional challenge and the July 2024 summary judgment motion in the District of South Carolina to the March 2025 $13.36 million erroneous-refund suit filed by the government and the April 1, 2025 jurisdictional dismissal leaving the dispute to the U.S. Tax Court—signals a permanent structural transformation in federal R&D tax credit enforcement. When evaluated alongside the Seventh Circuit's mandate in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner and the IRS's stringent business-component itemization requirements on the revised Form 6765, the government's position in the dispute signals that the era of substantiating multimillion-dollar enterprise research credit claims through high-level, post-period SME interviews and uncorroborated percentage estimates has decisively ended.

For corporate tax departments, tax controversy attorneys, and technical advisors operating in the United States, three overarching doctrinal imperatives govern defensible Section 41 practice going forward. First, narrative consultant studies do not constitute primary evidence; under IRC § 6001 and the Federal Rules of Evidence, an accounting firm's report is merely a secondary summary that, as the government argued in Kyocera AVX, cannot carry the taxpayer's burden on summary judgment unless backed by preserved, contemporaneous technical artifacts, original survey records, and invoice-level general ledger validation. Second, proving the Four-Part Test—and specifically the 80 percent process of experimentation threshold of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)—requires establishing a granular, subcomponent-level nexus between employee hours, experimental hypotheses, and pilot-model expenditures through real-time operational systems such as Jira, GitHub, PLM, and ERP platforms rather than after-the-fact memory reconstructions. Finally, taxpayers filing amended look-back refund claims must anticipate heightened IRS examination scrutiny, verify full compliance with jurisdictional prerequisites under IRC § 7422 and Flora, and implement ironclad litigation-hold retention protocols before submitting any claim to the federal government.

metaDescription: Kyocera AVX Components Corp. v. United States is a federal R&D tax credit dispute over a $1.3 million IRC Section 41 refund claim for 2018.
